newsitem.title: USA: Chemically-treated utility poles pose hazard-study.
newsitem.headline: Chemically-treated utility poles pose hazard-study.

text.p: Utilities should phase out the use of wooden utility poles that are usually treated with dangerous pesticides and wood preservatives, an environmental group said Tuesday.

"Under, around, in and on every preservative-treated utility pole is a toxic site that poses a real threat to clean air, water and land," a report by the National Coalition Against the Misuse of Pesticides said.
"Utility companies play a central role in either continuing or stopping the poisoning and contamination of the environment, their communities and ultimately their customers," it said.

Instead of using wooden poles, which are protected against decay by chemicals that are banned for many other uses, the coalition said utilities should use alternatives such a steel, concrete, fiberglass, or should bury the lines.

Bill Wemhoff, director of environmental and regulatory affairs with the American Public Power Association, said use of treated wooden poles "has been studied in the past and found not to be harmful. If there is new information I haven't seen it."
Wemhoff said alternatives probably would be more expensive. Also, he said, the report "doesn't say what you would do with the poles that are out there."

More than 100 million utility poles line U.S. streets and highways. They account for about 13 percent of the market for wood preservatives used to kill fungus and insects and retard decay, the report said.

The chemicals, which include pentachlorophenol, creosote, arsenic and chromium VI and contaminants including dioxin, "contain some of the most hazardous toxic contaminants on the market," the report said.
After a use-span of about 40 years, the poles usually are discarded in landfills or recycled into fence posts or landscaping material, continuing the contamination threat, it added.
